structure.title: I
structure.summary: In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg and rents a modest bungalow, seeking renewal and purpose as he begins learning the bond business; after driving by car to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, he attends dinner at their opulent Georgian Colonial home, where Tom delivers a racist rant from 'The Rise of the Coloured Empires,' Daisy makes a cryptic remark about wishing her daughter to be a 'beautiful little fool,' and a telephone call hints at Tom’s affair in New York, confirmed in confidence by Jordan Baker; later, in the crimson room, Daisy and Tom jokingly suggest marrying Nick to Jordan, Daisy vaguely references a conversation about the Nordic race, and when she presses Nick about rumors of his engagement to a girl out West, he denies it, revealing the gossip prompted his move East; as Nick walks to his car, he sees Gatsby standing alone in the dark, stretching his arms toward a distant green light across the bay before vanishing into the night.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York; when the train stops at the desolate Valley of Ashes, Tom forcibly pulls Nick off to meet Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, at her husband George Wilson’s run-down garage. Under the looming eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg’s faded billboard, Myrtle dismisses her spiritless husband and insists on joining Tom in New York, boarding a separate train car to avoid scrutiny. In New York, Myrtle buys a dog from a street vendor’s basket of puppies and takes a lavender taxicab to her cramped, cluttered apartment on 158th Street, where she hosts a gathering with her sister Catherine and neighbors Mr. and Mrs. McKee. Tom opens whisky from a locked bureau, and as the group becomes increasingly intoxicated, Myrtle transforms into a performative figure of hauteur, boasting of her aspirations—including a massage, a dog collar, and a wreath for her mother’s grave—while Catherine reveals Myrtle married George Wilson believing he was a gentleman. The evening erupts in violence when Tom breaks Myrtle’s nose with his open hand after she dares to chant Daisy’s name, triggering chaos as women rush to help and Mr. McKee awakens dazedly before leaving; Nick departs with Mr. McKee in the elevator and later finds himself alone in the cold, empty Pennsylvania Station at dawn, staring at the morning Tribune.

structure.title: III
characters_present: The drunken man with owl-eyed spectacles
structure.summary: On a Saturday evening shortly after seven, Nick Carraway arrives at Jay Gatsby’s sprawling Long Island mansion by car, entering a chaotic, opulent party fueled by arrivals via Rolls-Royce, station wagon, motorboat, and train. The estate brims with extravagant details—five crates of weekly fruit deliveries, a butler-operated juicer, canvas-lit gardens, and a full orchestra—as guests mingle anonymously, spreading rumors that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy. Nick Carraway reconnects with Jordan Baker, encounters eccentric figures like Lucille—who received a $265 gown from Gatsby after tearing hers—and witnesses a drunken man in the library marveling at the authenticity of Gatsby’s real books. At midnight, the party peaks with opera singers and champagne served in finger-bowl glasses, yet Gatsby remains unseen until Nick Carraway, seated at a table, is startled to learn the composed, smiling man beside him is Gatsby himself, who invites him to fly in his hydroplane the next morning before vanishing into a phone call. As revelry descends into chaos—chorus girls weeping with running mascara, marital fights erupting, and a coupé crashing into a wall—Nick Carraway observes Gatsby standing alone on the porch, sober and detached, while Owl Eyes claims he wasn’t driving and a dazed passenger emerges asking for a gas station; Nick Carraway departs as Gatsby gestures farewell under a faint moon. Later, reflecting on midsummer New York, Nick Carraway recalls his routine work at the Probity Trust, nightly study in the Yale Club’s library, and lonely walks home along Madison Avenue, where he imagines fleeting romantic connections amid the city’s twilight; he rekindles his acquaintance with Jordan Baker, discovering her dishonesty through her admission of lying about damaging a borrowed car and cheating in a golf tournament, and their conversation about driving reveals her belief that others must avoid her—a carelessness both troubling and alluring—while he remains emotionally tethered to weekly letters signed 'Love, Nick' addressed to a woman back home, vividly remembering her perspiration on her lip.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion erupts into a wild, glittering party filled with guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York who arrive by car, including the Chester Beckers, Leeches, Snells, Klipspringer, and dozens of others whose identities are known only through rumor and gossip; amid cocktails and flowers, guests speculate absurdly about Gatsby’s origins—nephew to Von Hindenburg, cousin to the devil—while remaining utterly ignorant of his true identity, as Nick Carraway reflects on their transience and hollow revelry. Later that day, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn, inviting him to lunch and revealing a meticulously constructed but dubious biography: claiming aristocratic Midwestern roots, Oxford education, wartime heroism in the Argonne, and decorations including a Montenegrin medal for valor, which he produces as evidence, while also requesting Nick Carraway’s help in arranging a meeting with Jordan Baker regarding a matter he refuses to disclose. At noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, a grotesque figure with hair growing from his nostrils and cuff buttons made of human molars, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal at the old Metropole and casually boasts of fixing the 1919 World Series, before Gatsby abruptly leaves for a phone call; Nick Carraway then spots Tom Buchanan in the restaurant, and their introduction causes Gatsby visible distress before he vanishes. In a flashback to October 1917, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Daisy Fay in her white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby in Louisville, watching their intense romantic connection before Daisy’s life unravels: she attempts to run away to say goodbye to a soldier, is forbidden by her family, and marries Tom Buchanan after a drunken breakdown on her wedding day, during which she clings to a letter and demands her pearl necklace be returned; years later, after moving to Chicago with Tom and their daughter, Daisy recognizes Gatsby’s name for the first time in years, prompting Jordan to recall that 1917 moment. Finally, at dusk, Nick Carraway and Jordan ride in a victoria through Central Park as children sing, and Jordan reveals Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could live across the bay, asking Nick Carraway to invite her to tea so he can visit unannounced—his quiet obsession, born of five years of longing, overwhelms Nick Carraway, who shifts focus from Gatsby’s quest to the presence of Jordan beside him as the lights of Fifty-Ninth Street glow above.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: The chapter begins with Nick returning home at 2 a.m. to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit and eerily silent; Gatsby invites him to Coney Island or a swim, but Nick declines, instead proposing to invite Daisy over for tea—a plan Gatsby eagerly but nervously supports. The next day, rain falls heavily as Gatsby sends a man to cut Nick’s grass and arrives at the tea in a white flannel suit, visibly shaken; when Daisy arrives in a large open car, Gatsby, overwhelmed, knocks over a mantelpiece clock, leading to an agonizing silence that dissolves into quiet intimacy as the rain stops and sunlight returns. Gatsby then insists Daisy tour his mansion, walking with her along the road rather than the shortcut by the Sound, where she marvels at the gardens’ jonquils, hawthorn, and plum blossoms. Inside, they pass through opulent, empty rooms—Marie Antoinette music-rooms, Restoration Salons, and period bedrooms—where Nick senses unseen guests and hears what he believes is the owl-eyed man’s ghostly laughter; Gatsby displays his collection of shirts—linen, silk, flannel—in vibrant colors, causing Daisy to sob into the fabric, moved by their beauty. Gatsby points out the green light at the end of Daisy’s dock, now diminished in meaning, and shows her photographs of Mr. Dan Cody and a young picture of himself in yachting attire, which she admires playfully. A phone call referencing Detroit interrupts their intimacy, but as the storm clears, Daisy whimsically wishes to put Gatsby inside a pink and golden cloud. Gatsby calls Klipspringer, who reluctantly plays piano, and as Nick attempts to leave, he finds Gatsby and Daisy emotionally reconnected, with Gatsby holding Daisy’s hand, utterly absorbed in her presence.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s mansion seeking a statement, revealing the extent of Gatsby’s growing public notoriety fueled by wild rumors, including claims he lives in a mobile house-boat along Long Island’s shore; this prompts a reflective recounting of Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz, a poor North Dakota farm boy who, at seventeen, rowed out to meet Dan Cody’s yacht anchored in Little Girl Bay, was taken under Cody’s wing, and spent five years traveling across continents aboard the Tuolomee in multiple roles, adopting Gatsby’s identity and abstaining from alcohol due to Cody’s drunken excesses, though he inherited nothing after Ella Kaye seized Cody’s fortune. Weeks later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and encounters Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arriving on horseback; Gatsby nervously invites them to stay for drinks and supper, but their cold indifference and Sloane’s abrupt departure prevent him from joining their planned dinner. Later that Saturday night, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is overwhelmed by the excess and vulgarity of West Egg, yet shares a quiet, intimate moment with Gatsby on Nick Carraway’s porch after dancing; Tom grows suspicious of Gatsby’s background, dismissing him as a bootlegger, while Daisy defends him by claiming he owns drugstores. That night, Gatsby confides in Nick Carraway his desperate wish to erase the past five years and have Daisy declare she never loved Tom, so they can restart their relationship as if nothing had happened — insisting he can repeat the past, recalling their first kiss under moonlight five years earlier.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On a broiling summer afternoon, Nick Carraway arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house and finds Gatsby waiting, having replaced his original servants with silent newcomers hired by Wolfsheim to conceal Daisy’s visits. Tension erupts as Daisy openly kisses Gatsby and declares her love in front of Tom, who reacts with stunned alarm. The group departs for New York in two cars — Daisy chooses to ride with Gatsby in his yellow coupé while Tom, Nick, and Jordan take Tom’s blue coupé — during which Tom reveals he has investigated Gatsby’s past and dismisses his Oxford claim as fraudulent. After stopping at Wilson’s garage near the ash-heaps, where Wilson — visibly ill and desperate — reveals his plan to move West with Myrtle, and Myrtle mistakes Jordan for Tom’s wife in a moment of jealous terror, the group arrives at the Plaza Hotel. There, a violent confrontation unfolds: Tom exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging ties to Meyer Wolfsheim, and Daisy, under pressure, admits she never loved Tom but cannot deny having loved him in the past, shattering Gatsby’s idealized vision. Tom orders them to leave together in Gatsby’s car, ending the confrontation. Later, Myrtle Wilson is struck and killed by a yellow car speeding from New York; Michaelis witnesses her running into the road as the vehicle flees without stopping. Tom and Nick arrive at the scene to find Wilson hysterical, and Tom insists he was not driving, producing his blue coupé as alibi. That night, Gatsby emerges from the shadows to tell Nick that Daisy was driving the car when Myrtle was killed, and he intends to take the blame; Nick watches from outside as Tom and Daisy sit quietly together in the kitchen, sharing food in an intimate, conspiratorial calm, while Gatsby stands vigil in the moonlight, watching Daisy’s window.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: The chapter unfolds across a single day and night, beginning with Nick Carraway’s sleepless night haunted by a foghorn and his dawn rush to Gatsby’s mansion after hearing a taxi arrive, where he finds Gatsby dejected after waiting all night for Daisy to appear at her window—she briefly stood there before turning off the light. Together, they search the dusty rooms of the mansion for cigarettes, and Gatsby, refusing to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal, reveals his past: how he met Daisy at her wealthy home under false pretenses of social standing, fell irrevocably in love with her illusion, and was later stranded at Oxford while she married Tom Buchanan after receiving a letter that shattered his hopes. On the final afternoon before Gatsby’s departure, the two share a silent, tender embrace by a fire, a moment of quiet intimacy that lingers as a memory of lost love. Later, Gatsby recounts his solitary return to Louisville on his last army pay, walking streets they once shared and feeling he left her behind as the city faded from view; he never used his pool all summer. At dawn, Nick Carraway declares Gatsby worth more than 'the whole damn bunch put together,' eliciting a radiant smile. Meanwhile, George Wilson, consumed by grief over Myrtle’s death and convinced she was murdered by the driver of a yellow car, wanders on foot from his garage to Port Roosevelt and Gad’s Hill, then arrives in West Egg asking for Gatsby’s house. At two o’clock, Gatsby dons his bathing suit, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage, and orders the damaged car left untouched; he carries it alone to the pool, where he is later shot by Wilson, whose body is found in the grass only after Gatsby’s corpse is discovered floating on the mattress, gently disturbed by ripples and leaves.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left to manage the chaotic aftermath as police, photographers, and curious onlookers swarm his mansion, while Catherine’s denial at the inquest erases any link between Myrtle and Gatsby, reducing Wilson to a dismissed 'madman.' Nick Carraway desperately tries to reach Daisy and Meyer Wolfshiem by phone and courier, receiving only silence or a cold letter from Wolfshiem refusing to attend, compounded by a mistaken long-distance call that confirms Gatsby’s isolation. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, frail and tearful, bundled in a cheap ulster; overwhelmed by his son’s mansion, he proudly shows Nick Carraway a childhood notebook detailing Gatsby’s self-improvement schedule and a photograph of the house, revealing the depth of Gatsby’s ambition. Nick Carraway struggles to arrange a funeral—Klipspringer declines due to a picnic, Wolfshiem refuses citing a personal rule against posthumous involvement—and only Gatz, Nick Carraway, a Lutheran minister, and servants attend as rain falls. In a final, poignant moment, the man with owl-eyed glasses, whom Nick Carraway last saw marveling at Gatsby’s books, appears unexpectedly in the drizzle at the cemetery, wiping rain from his glasses to view the grave and murmuring 'Amen to that' before lamenting that Gatsby was once surrounded by hundreds. After packing and selling his car, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s abandoned house at night, erasing an obscene word scrawled on the steps, then walks to the beach where he reflects on the island’s original wilderness and Gatsby’s futile belief in the green light, concluding with the metaphor of humanity striving against the current, pulled back into the past. Before leaving, he confronts Jordan Baker, who reveals she is engaged to another man; they exchange bitter words about dishonesty, ending with his quiet admission of age and self-awareness. Later, he encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary, and emotionally clings to a box of dog biscuits as proof of his grief; Nick Carraway recognizes Tom and Daisy as careless people who destroy lives, and despite revulsion, shakes Tom’s hand before watching him enter a jewelry store to buy a pearl necklace or cuff buttons.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, New York, seeking purpose in the bond business and renting a modest home beside the extravagant mansion of the enigmatic Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—wealthy, entitled residents of East Egg—Nick is introduced to a world of privilege and moral decay. He learns of Tom’s affair with Myrtle Wilson, a woman trapped in a loveless marriage in the desolate Valley of Ashes, and meets Jordan Baker, a cynical golf player who reveals Gatsby’s unspoken obsession with Daisy. One night, Nick witnesses Gatsby standing alone, reaching toward a green light across the bay, symbolizing his longing for a past he cannot reclaim. As Nick becomes entangled in Gatsby’s world, he learns through Jordan’s recounting of 1917 that Gatsby, once James Gatz, a poor North Dakota farm boy, reinvented himself after meeting Dan Cody and falling in love with Daisy during his brief military posting in Louisville, vowing to one day return to her as a man worthy of her world.

Gatsby’s lavish parties, attended by nameless elites who spread wild rumors about him, serve as a stage for his performance of wealth meant to attract Daisy. Nick facilitates a reunion between Gatsby and Daisy at his own home, where Gatsby’s nervous grandeur—showing off his shirts, his mansion, and his carefully constructed identity—briefly rekindles their romance. But beneath the surface, cracks emerge: Tom Buchanan, suspicious and resentful, investigates Gatsby’s past and exposes him as a bootlegger tied to Meyer Wolfsheim, a mobster who fixed the 1919 World Series. The tension culminates in a violent confrontation at the Plaza Hotel, where Daisy, under pressure, admits she once loved Tom but cannot deny her feelings for Gatsby—yet refuses to renounce her marriage entirely. That night, Myrtle Wilson is killed by a yellow car driven by Daisy, though Gatsby takes the blame. George Wilson, Myrtle’s husband and misled by Tom into believing Gatsby was both her lover and her murderer, descends into grief-fueled madness.

After Gatsby’s death, Nick is left to navigate the hollow aftermath: Gatsby’s funeral is nearly无人问津, attended only by his father, a minister, a few servants, and the owl-eyed man who once marveled at Gatsby’s books. Nick discovers in Gatz’s childhood notebook the boy’s relentless self-improvement schedule, revealing the depth of Gatsby’s ambition and sincerity beneath the facade. Jordan Baker, now engaged to another, dismisses Nick’s moral outrage, while Tom Buchanan coldly admits he told Wilson where to find Gatsby—justifying it as necessary. In a final moment of clarity, Nick walks to the beach where Gatsby once gazed at the green light, reflecting on the illusion of the American Dream and humanity’s futile struggle against the current of time and memory. He departs the East, disillusioned but alive, carrying with him the haunting image of a man who believed he could repeat the past—and the quiet truth that those who destroy lives, like Tom and Daisy, retreat into their wealth, untouched by consequence.
